opus-5.5.text:
That's something I think about a lot, honestly. When I started as a faculty member, I had this worry that I'd have to give up coding entirely, because that's the stereotype: you become a professor, and suddenly your job is writing grants and reviewing papers. And coding has always been the thing that grounds me. It's how I think through problems.

But what I've come to realize is that the two don't have to be in competition. The way I see it, my first priority is always the students. They're at a stage where the right support at the right moment can change the trajectory of their whole career, so if a student is stuck or needs to talk through an idea, that comes first. But supporting students doesn't only mean meetings. A lot of the time, the most useful thing I can do is actually get my hands dirty alongside them. If we're building a system together, like we did with TVM or some of the machine learning compilation work, I can write a prototype, sketch out an abstraction, or review their code in a really detailed way. That's a form of mentorship too. Students learn a lot from seeing how you structure something, not just from hearing you describe it.

I also try to be careful not to take over. There's a temptation, when you can code, to just jump in and do it yourself because it's faster. But that robs the student of the chance to own the work. So I try to pick the pieces where my involvement helps unblock things or sets a direction, and then let them run with it and make it their own.

Practically, I protect some time for deep work. Maybe it's late at night or on weekends, when there are fewer meetings, and I'll just sit down and code. It keeps me sharp and connected to what's actually happening in the systems we build. And I think that makes me a better advisor, because I understand the real pain points instead of just talking about them abstractly.

So it's less about balancing two competing things and more about finding the place where they reinforce each other. Coding keeps me honest, and the students keep me growing. Seeing them become independent researchers who build things far beyond what I'd have imagined is ultimately the most rewarding part.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says students are the first priority and that their needs come before his own coding.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as deep work that supports his research and advising, but does not frame it as a hobby.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because I'm not willing to give up either one.

I'll start with the honest part: I still write code, and I don't think that's something I should apologize for. A lot of what I care about, whether it's TVM or XGBoost or the machine learning compilation work we've been doing, started because I sat down and built something myself and discovered what was hard. If I stopped touching the code entirely, I think my intuition about what problems are worth solving would degrade pretty quickly. You lose the feel for where the friction actually is.

But I've also come to see that the way I code has to change once you have students. When I was a student, writing code was the whole job. Now I think of it more as a way of staying grounded. I'll prototype something to understand it, or dig into a performance problem because it's bothering me, but I try not to be the person who owns the critical path of a student's project. That's their work. If I take over, I'm robbing them of the thing they actually came here to learn.

So the prioritization, in practice, looks like this. Students come first in terms of time commitments. If someone needs to talk through a design, or is stuck, or has a paper deadline, that takes precedence over anything I wanted to hack on. The coding fits into the gaps, and sometimes into evenings, and I've just accepted that it's a smaller fraction of my week than it used to be.

What makes it work, I think, is that a lot of my coding happens in the open, in the same codebases my students work in. So it's not really separate from supporting them. If I'm reviewing a pull request or fixing something in the compiler infrastructure, that's me staying close enough to the system that I can give useful advice, rather than advice from memory of how things used to work. Being a useful collaborator is a form of mentorship.

And the other thing I'd say is that building a community around the projects helps a lot. Open source means I'm not the only person my students can learn from. They get feedback from contributors all over the world, and that scales in a way my personal time never could.

So the short answer is that students are the priority, but I keep coding deliberately, in a way that serves them rather than competes with them. I find that when I get that balance right, both sides get better.

r001.rationale: It says students come first in time commitments and their needs take precedence over coding.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as a way to stay grounded and support students, not as a hobby.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as connected. Supporting students means helping them build the confidence and judgment to pursue their own ideas. Sometimes that means working through a technical problem together; sometimes it means stepping back and giving them room to figure it out.

I still want to stay close to the code because it helps me ask better questions and understand where the hard parts are. But I have to be careful that my enthusiasm for solving a problem doesn’t take away their opportunity to solve it. So I would prioritize helping the student move forward, and find ways for my own coding to support that.

r001.rationale: It says he would prioritize helping the student move forward and keep his own coding in support of that.

r002.rationale: It describes wanting to stay close to the code as useful to mentoring, not as a hobby.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of supporting students as a very important part of my job, so I try to make sure they have the feedback and direction they need. But that doesn’t mean I need to solve every problem for them. You want to give students room to develop their own ideas and become independent researchers.

For me, coding is also a way to think. When you actually implement something, you discover details that you might miss in a discussion. So I try to keep some time for that, and bring what I learn back into conversations with students. There’s a balance, but the two activities can really help each other.

r001.rationale: The response calls student support important and describes balancing it with coding, but it does not place student support above Tianqi Chen’s personal desire to code.

r002.rationale: It describes coding as a way to think and learn; it does not frame coding as a hobby.
